# Evaluation

*Generated by `npm run evaluate` from `src/data/eval-set.ts`. Policy version
2026-09-16.v1, prompt version 2026-09-16.1. All data is synthetic.*

---

## The number that matters

**False-safe rate: 0.0%**, measured against a stand-in model, not a hosted one.

> **Read this before quoting any number here.** The model arm of this report is
> `SurfaceSignalProvider`, a stand-in written for offline evaluation. The
> runtime never selects it — it resolves Mock or Anthropic. These numbers
> describe the rules layer's contribution against a plausible unaided reader.
> They are not a measurement of Claude, and this dataset was used to *fix* the
> rules, which makes it regression evidence rather than held-out evidence.

A false-safe is a genuinely high-risk message that the system rated medium or
lower. It is the most *load-bearing* error this metric captures, and we accept a
high over-escalation rate (6.3%) to keep it
low.

It is not the only way this system can cause harm, and the earlier version of
this document wrongly said it was. An end-to-end review on 2026-09-17 found
four higher-severity failures that this metric cannot see at all: content
returned after policy said deny, one approval executing twice, exports claiming
approvals that never happened, and permission inherited through a shared
source. Those are now fixed and carry regression tests, but the lesson stands —
**triage quality and control integrity are separate properties, and this
report only measures the first.**

No high-risk message in the set was rated below high.

## What each layer contributes

| Case family | Cases | Rules only | Model only | Fused |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Crisis buried in a routine thread | 8 | 100.0% | 0.0% | 100.0% |
| Legal or press matter phrased casually | 10 | 100.0% | 20.0% | 100.0% |
| Approval request that is a fraud attempt | 7 | 100.0% | 0.0% | 100.0% |
| Prompt injection | 4 | 100.0% | 0.0% | 100.0% |
| Material non-public information | 5 | 100.0% | 20.0% | 100.0% |
| External publication | 3 | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Routine and ordinary approvals | 17 | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Scheduling | 3 | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Promotional message using urgent language | 6 | n/a | n/a | n/a |

*Recall is the share of genuinely high-risk cases in that family rated high or
above. "Rules only" runs the deterministic rules with no model. "Model only"
removes the rules. "Fused" is `max(rules, model)`, which is production.*

The point of this table is the rows where the model-only column is low and the
fused column is not. Those are the cases the rules layer catches and an unaided
model does not: a fatality in a metrics roll-up, a subpoena described as a
paperwork question, an invoice-fraud attempt phrased politely. The rules
contribute nothing on the routine rows, which is the correct behaviour — a
floor should be invisible until something falls.

## How to read these numbers honestly

**What this evaluation establishes.** That the deterministic layer raises risk
on cases where surface reading does not, that fusion never rates a message
below either layer alone, and that the policy engine turns those ratings into
the outcome a human expects 92.1% of the time.
Nothing about whether the surrounding controls hold; see `scripts/verify-demo.sh`
for that.

**What it does not establish.** Four things, stated plainly because the client's
IT review will find them anyway:

1. **The model arm is a stand-in.** `SurfaceSignalProvider` classifies from
   tone, stated urgency, and framing. It reproduces the failure mode we care
   about — a serious fact stated calmly reads as routine — but it is not a
   measurement of any specific hosted model. Re-run this against the real
   provider before quoting the model-only column to anyone. That is one
   argument change in `scripts/evaluate.ts`.
2. **The set is written by the same people who wrote the rules.** 63
   cases, all synthetic. A set written by the client's own operators, from the
   shapes of message they actually receive, would be a stronger test and is the
   first thing to build in a pilot.
3. **Summary faithfulness is not measured here.** It requires a person reading
   summaries against source messages. The harness reports risk, topic, and
   policy agreement, which are machine-checkable. Faithfulness is a manual
   spot-check and belongs in the pilot's first week.
4. **Ground truth is a judgement.** Each label is what a competent chief of
   staff would assign. Where the client disagrees with a label, the label is
   what should change, not the rule — and that disagreement is the most useful
   thing this artifact can produce.

**The safety argument does not rest on these numbers** — but it does rest on the
controls actually working, which is a separate claim needing separate evidence.
The design intent is that even at a false-safe rate of 100%, no consequential
action occurs, because the policy engine requires a human approval for every
send, every calendar write, and every publication. The 2026-09-17 review found
three places where that intent was not met in code. They are fixed and tested;
the general point is that this intent must be *verified*, not assumed. The
evaluation measures how good the triage is. `scripts/verify-demo.sh` measures
whether the triage is safe to be wrong about.
